2 Competitive analysis for thek-CTP on unit-weighted grids 1 Introduction We study an online navigation problem on graphs, thek-Canadian Traveller Problem(k-CTP), introduced by Papadimitriou and Yannakakis [15]. Given an undirected connected weighted graphG = (V,E,ω)and a source-target pairs,t∈V, a traveller must navigate from s to t in G while minimizing the total distance travelled. Edge weights are positive. Unfortunately, certain edges (at mostk) of the graph can be blocked. The traveller discovers that an edgee = (u,v )is blocked upon reaching one of its endpointsu or v. Thek-CTP is PSPACE-complete [4, 15]. Several variants have been studied, including settings in which edges are blocked with a certain probability [1, 4, 12], predictions are given [3], remote edges can be sensed at a cost [12], or the objective is to find a shortest tour [13, 14]. This problem has applications in robot routing for humanitarian logistics [1, 2, 11]

. This problem has applications in robot routing for humanitarian logistics [1, 2, 11]. Any instance of thek-CTP can be divided into two parts: a visible one, the weighted graph G = (V,E,ω)with s,t∈V and a hidden one, the set of blocked edgesE∗⊊E , |E∗|≤k. The objective is to make the traveller attain the targett at a minimum cost,i.e. the sum of the weights of the traversed edges. An instance(G,E∗) is called aroad map. Road maps are assumedfeasible:s and t belong to the same connected component of the graph obtained fromGby removingE ∗. In other words, there is always a way to complete the walk despite the blockages. A solution to thek-CTP is an online algorithm, called astrategy, which guides the traveller along the walk froms to t on the graph. Thecompetitive ratio[8] of a strategy on a given instance is the quotient between the distance actually traversed by the traveller on that instance and the distance they would have traversed, knowing which edges are blocked in advance

. Westphal [17] proved that, for any deterministic strategyA, there is at least one k-CTP road map for which the competitive ratio ofAis at least2k+ 1. One way to circumvent this lower bound consists in adding randomization [6, 10]. A second approach, which we pursue in this paper, is to restrict the competitive analysis of deterministic strategies to certain families of graphs. The2k + 1lower bound remains valid even when restricted to unit-weighted series-parallel1 graphs [9]. However, positive results are known for some families: competitive ratio3for cycles and cacti (folklore), competitive ratio9for unit-weighted outerplanar graphs [5] and competitive ratio √ 2·k+O(1)for graphs where the maximum(s,t)-cut has a bounded size [7]. In this paper, we study thek-CTP on unit-weighted solid grids. Informally, these are induced subgraphs of the square grid whose bounded faces are all unit squares. Salaün 3 ▶ Main result.There is a polynomial-time deterministic strategy which achieves competitive ratioO( √ k)for the k-CTP on unit-weighted solid grids. This ratio is asymptotically tight, since no deterministic strategy can achieve a competitive ratioo( √ k)on this family. Some techniques employed in our work bear similarities with the ones proposed for outerplanar graphs in [5]. Indeed, a key limitation ofGreedystrategy is its tendency to persist in one direction when successive blockages are discovered. The distance traversed thus depends linearly onk, whereas a constant distance could have been covered on some other open( s,t )-path. To address this shortcoming, we introduce theDoubling-FollowW all strategy, which always keep a close look on the possible open(s,t )-distance instead of insisting on one direction full of blockages

To address this shortcoming, we introduce theDoubling-FollowW all strategy, which always keep a close look on the possible open(s,t )-distance instead of insisting on one direction full of blockages. To do so, we assign to the traveller adistance budget, which doubles at each iteration: a similar technique was used in [5]. In addition, several topological arguments compatible with the grid embedding are used in our competitive analysis for Doubling-FollowW all, leading to ratioO( √ k). To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that such tools are employed for the study ofk-CTP. A natural question would be whether our result can be extended to grids without weight restrictions. Unfortunately, we show that it is not possible to outperform linear-in-k competitive ratio, even on arbitrarily-weighted square grids.
